father,   the   late   Sheikh   Zayed   bin   Sultan Al   Nahyan. As   a   federally   funded   public   institution,
UAEU graduated its first cohort of students in 1981 and now proudly boasts 79,372 alumni.

within the UAE and internationally.

## PDF page 42
The newly established Stem Cells Research Center, located in the College of Medicine and Health Sciences, aims
to become a pioneering hub for advancing regenerative medicine and personalized healthcare in the region. The
center   will   focus   on   disease   modelling,   therapeutic   development,   and   innovation   using   stem   cell   technologies,
with  applications  ranging  from  cardiovascular  and  neurodegenerative  diseases  to  diabetes,  cancer,  and  rare  ge-
netic  disorders.  Its  objectives  include  developing  accurate  patient-derived  disease  models,  advancing  personal-
ized    medicine    through    iPSC    technology,    and    accelerating    the    translation    of    laboratory    discoveries    into    clinical
practice.    Equipped   with    cutting-edge    infrastructure    such    as    gene-editing    systems,    bioreactors,    high-resolution
imaging,        and        bioinformatics        platforms,        the        center       will        foster        interdisciplinary        collaboration        across        academia,
healthcare,  and  industry.  It will  also  play  a  key  role  in  training  the  next  generation  of  researchers  and  clinicians,
building local capacity, and contributing to the UAE’s leadership in biomedical innovation. Ultimately, the center
is envisioned as a catalyst for improving patient outcomes, generating economic and social benefits, and position-
ing UAEU as a regional leader in stem cell research and therapeutic development.

The  Public  Health  Genotoxicology  lab was  established  as  the  first  lab  of  the  IPH,  the  first  genotoxicology  lab  at
the UAEU, and one of the very few in the country. It applies to one of the most sensitive genotoxicity tests, the
single-cell  gel  electrophoresis  assay  or  comet  assay,  which  is  planned  to  be  completed  with  other  assays  in  the
future. The lab is equipped with the Metafer automated image analysis system, the first of its kind in the Region.
The lab is well-suited for running in vitro studies characterizing the DNA-damaging properties of environmental
chemical     exposures.     Currently,     the     genotoxicity     of    various     pesticide-active     ingredients     is     compared     to     that     of
traditional  and  encapsulated  product  formulations.  In  addition,  preparations  are  underway  to  start  genotoxico-
logical  biomonitoring  and  biobanking  in  the  Mutaba’ah  Mother  and  Child  Study,  the  sample  collection  of which
will begin early next year.

ical  research  on  infectious  diseases  to  assess  burden,  risk  factors,  and  interventions,  collaborating with  experts
to strengthen the UAE’s response to disease outbreaks and build research capacity. 3. Implementation Research
Unit  (IRU)  IRU  strengthens  health  systems  through  operational  research  that  informs  policy,  improves  program

building at the program level. 4. Health Education Research Unit (HERU) HERU advances health education with

health  infrastructure,  advancing  research  capabilities,  and  positioning  the  UAEU  as  a  leader  in  addressing  com-
plex health challenges locally and globally.

## PDF page 43
to     initiate     the     recruitment     of     a     specialized     consultant     for     the     planned     building     upgrade     and     the     development
of   a   new   facility.  This   milestone   reflects   the   College’s   proactive   response   to   unprecedented   growth   in   student
enrollment,  with   MD   intake   rising   by   more   than   765%   since   the   establishment   of   the   current   building   in   1995,
alongside     the     addition     of     14     new     programs     across     medicine     and     health     sciences.    The     consultant    will     provide
expert  guidance  in  designing  state-of-the-art  teaching,  research,  and  student  support  facilities,  aligned with  in-
ternational accreditation standards. This step marks a critical advancement in ensuring CMHS not only alleviates
current overcrowding but also strengthens its position as the nation’s oldest and most prestigious medical school,
committed to excellence, innovation, and the holistic success of its diverse student body.

The   College   has   successfully   implemented   a   comprehensive   digitalization   strategy,   fundamentally   transforming
educational    delivery,    student    engagement,    and    administrative    efficiency.    On    the    academic    side,    CMHS    has    in-
troduced a fully integrated educational portal, an AI-enhanced assessment system that provides dynamic perfor-
mance   analytics,   and   a   secure   online   exam   platform   that   strengthens   reliability   and   integrity.   For   students,   the
development of a unified student portal and a dedicated student affairs portal has improved access to academic
portfolios,    mentorship    programs,    calendars,    event    registration,    and    support    services,    greatly    enriching    the    stu-
dent    experience.   Administratively,    the    college    has    adopted    a    faculty    KPI    system    that    aligns    performance    with

a    comprehensive    procurement    platform    (MSR)    that    brings    transparency    and    accountability    to    requisitions    and
budget   tracking.   Collectively,   these   achievements   have   created   an   interconnected,   data-driven   ecosystem   that
enhances    quality,    fosters    innovation,    and    positions    CMHS    as    a    national    leader    in    digital    transformation   within
medical education.

The UAEU Genomics Laboratory, affiliated with the department, achieved a remarkable 99% score on the College
of   American     Pathologists     (CAP)     Proficiency   Test.   This     success     underscores     its     technical     excellence     and     moves
the  lab  closer  to  full  CAP  accreditation. As  a  national  center  of  excellence,  the  laboratory  plays  a  crucial  role  in
research, diagnostics, and education. Its focus  includes  rare genetic diseases, and it has identified over 400 dis-
ease-causing  mutations,  helping  to  pave  the way  for  new  therapeutic  and  preventive  strategies. The  lab  boasts

advanced technologies like Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS), mass spectrometry, and a multidisciplinary team
of geneticists, counselors, and bioinformaticians.

In      the      2024/25      academic     year,      the      College      secured      a      significant      budget      allocation      of      20      million      dirhams      for
equipment   purchase   to   enhance   its   teaching   and   research   infrastructure. This   strategic   investment   reflects   the
institution’s strong commitment to academic excellence and innovation. The primary objective was to strengthen
the  College’s  capacity  to  deliver  high-quality  education  and  support  advanced  research  through  the  acquisition
of modern laboratory and  clinical  equipment. The  funding  enabled  the  purchase  of state-of-the-art  instruments
for   the   Nutrition   and   Health   and   Speech-Language   Pathology   departments,   significantly   improving   the   quality,
efficiency, and range of academic and research activities conducted in these disciplines. The Doctor of Medicine
(MD)   program   also   benefited   substantially   from   this   initiative,  with   outdated   equipment   replaced   by   advanced
technologies  that  meet  international  standards  in  medical  education  and  training. These  upgrades  not  only  en-
hanced students’ hands-on learning experiences but also ensured that the curriculum remains aligned with global
best practices. Overall, the 20 million dirhams investment has strengthened the College’s research and teaching
capabilities, elevated the quality of student learning, and reinforced the institution’s position as a leading center
for health sciences education and research in the region.

Academic Programs and Curriculum:

New program: Master’s of Clinical Research

The  College  of  Medicine  and  Health  Sciences  (CMHS),  Depar tment  of  Internal  Medicine,  established  a  Master
of      Science      program      in      Clinical      Research      to      provide      in-depth      knowledge      and      prac tical      skills      in      all      aspect s      of
clinical sciences  research.  The  program  is  intended  to  enable  clinicians  and  health  care  professionals  to  reflect
critically on clinical and operational workplace experiences, gain insights into healthcare issues and challenges,
find  solutions  to  overcome  those  challenges,  improve  patient  outcomes,  enhance  the  health  of  the  public,  and
reduce the burdens of illness and disabilit y. The program is structured to address the current unmet need for
building    research    capacit y    among    clinicians    and    health    care    professionals    in    various    healthcare    organizations
in the UAE, as evidenced by request s from the National Institutes of Health and UAE health authorities to en -
hance clinicians’ research skills in clinical epidemiological and health ser vices research.


Updates and Improvements to existing programs, Accreditation and assessment outcomes

The   college’s   programs   have   secured   C A A   Re-accreditation   in   the   2024/2025   academic   year.   The   undergrad-
uate  programs  under went  a  curriculum  reform  in  general  education  to  align  with  the  current  national  require -
ment s.     The     updated     framework     emphasizes     key     themes     such     as     UAE     National     Identit y,     Academic     L anguage
Proficiency,  Innovation,  Entrepreneurship,  Sustainabilit y,  Quantitative  Reasoning  and  Critical  Thinking,  as  well
as     exposure     to     the     Humanities,     Behavioral     and     Social     Sciences,     Natural     Sciences,     Health     and     Wellness,     and
Cultural Diversity.

                                                                        In addition, the Doc tor of Medicine program under went a com-
                                                                        prehensive         curriculum         reform,         marking         a         significant         shift         to-
                                                                        ward      competency-based      medical      education      in      alignment      with
                                                                        the               EmiratesMEDs               framework               and               CA A               recommendations.
                                                                        The           new           curriculum           introduces           integrated,           patient-centered,
                                                                        and     spiral     courses     from     the     first     year,     with     longitudinal     tracks
                                                                        that           provide           early           clinical           exposure.           Traditional           lectures           are

Outreach programs and community service projects

The Department of Obstetrics and
Gynecology          at          CMHS,          UAEU,          ac-
tively participated in the UAE’s Year
of       Community       initiative       as       part       of
its         commitment         to         national         prior-
ities         and         community         engagement.
In alignment with this initiative, the
Department successfully integrat-
ed        the        Medical        Students        Commu-
nity            Campaign            into            the            OB/GYN
clerkship curriculum. During their
clinical                     rotations,                     students                    were
engaged in designing and leading
health awareness campaigns ad-
dressing key obstetrics and gyne-
cology               topics,               including               maternal
health,       reproductive       wellness,       and
disease prevention.

Through this initiative, students gained valuable hands-on experience in public  health education, cultural sensi-
tivity,   and   community   engagement,  while   contributing   meaningfully   to   raising   health   awareness   and   improving
health    literacy    across    the    UAE.   The    campaigns    utilized    evidence-based,    culturally    appropriate    approaches    and
provided   students  with   opportunities   to   develop   communication   and   leadership   skills   in   real-world   community
settings.

Overall,      the      initiative      strengthened      the      connection      between      CMHS      and      the     wider      community,      fostered      sus-
tainable   partnerships  with   local   organizations,   and   generated   a   lasting   positive   impact   on   public   health.   It   also
reinforced the College’s role in supporting national health promotion efforts and advancing experiential learning
aligned with the UAE’s strategic vision for community well-being.

MD students participate both individually and through the highly active Student Health & Promotion Committee
(HPSC) to engage with the UAE community in various awareness campaigns. They collaborate with influential or-
ganizations and healthcare institutions such as Zayed Higher Organization, Al Ain Football Club, Tawam Hospital,
and multiple schools across Al Ain. Through these initiatives, CMHS students reach diverse community segments,
including children, youth, adults, and older generations. Their community service projects and workshops address
a  wide   range  of  topics,   including  Cervical   and  Breast   Cancer,  Obesity,  Bullying,   the Journey  of  Pregnancy,  Stop
the Bleed, Diabetes, World Hearing Day, World Cancer Day, Language Disorders Awareness Month, and Autism
Spectrum Day, among others. See Appendix 1 for pictures.

Dr.   Iffat   Elbarazi,  Associate   Professor   of   Public   Health,  was   appointed   in   October   2024   as   the   National   Repre-
sentative for the UNESCO Chair on Global Health and Education. This high-profile appointment will provide the
opportunity to contribute to a global dialogue, bridging the gap between health and education and advocating for

individuals through health literacy by building networks between educators, policymakers, health professionals,

ucation.

## PDF page 59
During   the   2024/25   academic  year,   significant   challenges   arose   following   the   procurement   policy   changes   im-
plemented   in  April   2025.  The   transition   period   led   to   a   temporary   freeze   on   most   procurement   activities   until
the    university’s    procurement    team    released    updated    guidelines.    Unfortunately,    the    prolonged    clarification    and
approval    process    caused    notable    delays    in    ordering    essential    equipment,    supplies,    and    services,    which    in    turn
impacted the timely execution of several academic and research initiatives.

The introduction of new approval requirements from the Provost, University Operations Department (UOD), and
the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) for organizing events, workshops, and conferences involving internation-
al   participants   created   a   substantial   administrative   burden   for   the   College.  The   multi-layered   approval   process
significantly increased the time needed to plan and execute events, often resulting in delays and, in some cases,
the     cancellation     of     scheduled     activities.    These     procedural     complexities     limited     the     College’s     ability     to     engage
promptly with external partners and host international academic and research collaborations.

The  College  continues  to  grow,  with  an  increasing  number  of  programs  and  a  steadily  expanding  student  base.
While every effort is made to maintain a balanced faculty-to-student ratio, the College faces ongoing challenges
in recruiting and retaining qualified faculty, as compensation packages have remained unchanged over the years.
Additionally,     hiring     adequate     support     staff     has     become     increasingly     difficult,     adversely     affecting     the     College’s
overall operations and its ability to sustain the desired quality of teaching and academic support.

The experiences of the 2024/25 academic year highlighted critical operational and strategic lessons as the Col-
lege  of  Medicine  and  Health  Sciences  continued  to  expand  in  scale,  scope,  and  impact.  Challenges  arising  from
procurement policy changes, extended approval processes for international engagement, and constraints in fac-
ulty  and  staff  recruitment  underscored  the  growing  complexity  of  operating within  an  evolving  regulatory  envi-
ronment. These challenges emphasized the need for stronger alignment between academic planning, institutional
governance,  and  national  compliance  frameworks  to  ensure  continuity  in  education,  research,  and  external  en-
gagement during periods of transition.

In response, CMHS will adopt a more integrated and anticipatory planning approach that aligns academic, research,
and operational timelines with university-level and national processes. Strategic priorities include strengthening
coordination with central administrative units, implementing structured annual procurement and event-planning
cycles, and leveraging digital platforms to enhance transparency, efficiency, and decision-making. In parallel, the

## PDF page 59 — continuation 2
College  will   continue   to   advocate   for   sustainable   faculty   and  workforce   planning   models   that   support   Emirati-
zation  objectives,  improve  recruitment  and  retention,  and  maintain  high-quality  teaching  and  academic  support
amid continued program and enrollment growth.

Looking   forward,   CMHS  will   focus   on   consolidating   its   role   as   a   leading   national   and   regional   academic   health
sciences institution in alignment with UAE Vision 2031, the National Strategy for Wellbeing, and national health-
care  and  innovation  agendas.  Future  plans  include  targeted  investments  in  infrastructure  expansion,  faculty  ca-
pacity    building,    and    translational    research    that    addresses    national    health    priorities.    By    embedding    the    lessons
learned into its governance and strategic frameworks, the College aims to enhance institutional resilience, enable
sustainable growth, and deliver long-term value to the UAE’s healthcare system and knowledge-based economy.

Continued     investment     in     teaching     and     research     infrastructure,     including     new     and     upgraded     laboratories     such
as the Digital Fabrication and Model-Making Lab, Building Energy & Materials Lab, Unit Operations and Drilling
Labs, and advanced computer laboratories.

Enhanced research infrastructure supporting projects in artificial intelligence, renewable energy, water resources,
materials science and aerospace engineering.

Smart classrooms and learning technologies with interactive teaching spaces and improved virtual-learning plat-
forms.

Campus enhancements completed in 2025 provided additional student collaboration spaces and renovated lab-
oratory facilities, together with updated safety protocols.

Extensive laboratory network: COE operates 44 scientific laboratories that support hands-on learning, prototyp                                                                                                                    -
ing and research. These facilities span electronics, mechatronics, robotics, vibration analysis, unit operations and
drilling, providing a strong infrastructure for both theoretical and applied engineering.




Student enrolment: Headcounts    increased        from    3007    students    in    Fall    2020    to    3949    students    in    Fall    2025    as
graduation rates rose and admissions became more selective.

Graduation    rates:    On-time    graduation    rates    remained    high    across    bachelor’s,    master’s    and    doctoral    programs.
Employment rates within nine months of graduation exceeded 85 % for most programs.

Student demographics:   Female   students   comprised   57%   of   the   graduating   class.   Emirati   nationals   represented
roughly 90% of undergraduates, with the remainder being international students.

Diversity    initiatives:     The    College    continued    outreach    to    schools    in   Al   Ain    and    the    broader    UAE    to    attract    un-
der-represented groups.




New programs: Introduction of the PhD in Environmental Engineering and Minor in Environmental Engineering;
approval  of  the  PhD  in Water  Resources  for  launch  in  Fall  2025;  planned  Minor  in  Climate  Change  and  Sustain-
ability.

Program updates: Curricula in existing undergraduate and graduate programs were revised to incorporate emerg-
ing technologies and sustainability topics.

Accreditation:    Sevel    of    eight    undergraduate    programs    maintain    accreditation    by   ABET.    Preparations    for    forth-
coming re-accreditation reviews are underway.

Interdisciplinary          initiatives:           The          College          continues          to          promote          multidisciplinary          collaboration          through          joint
courses and research projects with other colleges.

flects   the   university’s   diverse   community   of   over   20,000   students   from   more   than   80   nationalities.  Within   the
Bachelor of Veterinary Medicine (BVM) program, mixed-gender and multicultural classes have been institutional  -
ized since 2019 under a special Chancellor’s exemption, enabling equitable access to veterinary education for all
qualified students. The department’s faculty and student body represent a wide spectrum of cultural, ethnic, and
professional backgrounds,  enriching  the  academic  environment  and promoting intercultural competence. These
efforts      align      with      UAEU’s      strategic      goal      of      designing      enriching      and      engaging      student      journeys      that      embrace
tolerance,  ethical  professionalism,  and  respect  for  diversity.  Student  support  structures—including  the  Students
of   Determination   Services,   the   Student   Success   Unit,   and   the   Career   and Alumni   Center—ensure   equitable   op-
portunities for learning, wellbeing, and professional development, further embedding the principles of diversity,
inclusion, and mutual respect across the academic experience.

Food Science Department
During     the     2024–2025     academic    year,     the     Food     Science     Department     significantly     upgraded     its     research     and
instructional facilities to enhance the quality of teaching, learning, and innovation.

Major upgrades included the refurbishment of the Food Science Research Laboratories, with dedicated facilities
for Fermentation and Enzyme Technology and a Dairy Pilot Plant.

Advanced     analytical     instruments    were     procured     and     commissioned,     notably     the     HPLC-MS,     GC-MS,     Rheome-
ter,      and     Texture     Analyzer,      alongside      a      Binder      incubator,     which      collectively      expand      the      department’s      capacity
for  advanced  food  analysis,  metabolomics,  and  sensory  research. These  upgrades  contribute  directly  to  the  de-
partment’s  mission  of  fostering  sustainable   food  systems   and  align  with   the  UAE   Food  Security  Strategy  2051.
They  also  strengthen  the  department’s  ability  to  support   multidisciplinary  collaborations  with   national  industry
partners, including Agthia and Al Ain Dairy.

                                                                                                   work,   and   all   required   documents   were   sub-
                                                                                                   mitted           for           tendering,           marking           a           major           ad-
                                                                                                   vancement toward the renovation phase.

                                                                                                   Additionally,                  the                  College                  inaugurated                  the
                                                                                                   Genomic Research Unit under the leadership
                                                                                                   of Dr. Moneeb Qablan. This AED 5 million fa-
                                                                                                   cility       enhances       the       UAE’s       national       research
capacity in molecular genetics, zoonotic disease control, and biodiversity conservation. It supports cutting-edge

genomic   investigations   aligned  with   the   “One   Health”   initiative,   strengthening   the   UAE’s   global   position   in   ad-

ordinated   through   a   dedicated   Campus   Committee,   ensuring   that   both   staff   and   students   benefit   from   a   safe,
efficient, and modern educational environment.


Integrative Agriculture Department
The        Department        of        Integrative       Agriculture        upgraded        its        research        and        teaching        infrastructure        extensively        in
2024–2025  to  enhance  scientific  excellence  and  student  experience.  Key  updates  include  the  installation  of  an
ICP-MS Model 7850, enabling ultra-trace detection and quantification of elements for environmental and biolog-
ical research. Laboratory safety was reinforced through the installation of Chemical and Acid Safety Boxes, while
a  Laboratory  Grinder  and  Millipore  Ultra-Pure Water  System were  procured  to  improve  analytical  accuracy  and
workflow efficiency. Anatomical model collections were expanded to support practical courses in Animal Science
and  Marine  Fisheries,  offering  detailed  visualizations  of  ruminant  and  poultry  anatomy  to  facilitate  experiential
learning. The department also undertook improvements to its farm-based research facilities, providing upgraded
resources for ongoing research and student projects.

Research Farm
The    Research    Farms    Stations    achieved    significant    progress    in    research-oriented    infrastructure    and    sustainable
agricultural   technology.   Key   projects   include   the   establishment   of   a   Hive   Bees   Project   at  Al   Foah   Farm   (2024),
supporting ecological research in pollination and biodiversity.

The      launch      of      the      Greenhouse      Smart      Irrigation      System      Project,      in      collaboration     with      private      sector      partners,
introduced   the   region’s   first   IoT-based   irrigation   control   system,   reducing  water   consumption   by   approximately
40%. This system integrates soil and environmental sensors to enable precision farming, automated alerts, and re-
al-time data-driven irrigation management. Additional infrastructure initiatives include upgrades for experimen   -
tal  fields,  animal  research  units,  and  facilities  supporting  25  concurrent  research  projects  across  plant,  soil,  and
livestock systems. Launch of a new graduate program: the MSc in Functional and Sustainable Foods, designed to
produce skilled professionals capable of advancing food security and sustainability goals in the UAE and beyond.

Notable student research, projects, or extracurricular accomplishments
A    student    research    team    developed    a    new    generation    of    heat-resistant    biopesticides    aimed    at    controlling    the
Red     Palm     Weevil     (Rhynchophorus      ferrugineus)—one      of     the      most      destructive     pests      affecting      date     palms.    This
innovative project focuses on enhancing the stability and effectiveness of biopesticides under high-temperature
conditions typical of the UAE’s environment. The research contributes to sustainable pest management, reducing
reliance on chemical pesticides and supporting the long-term health and productivity of the country’s date palm
industry.

         suppor ting the adoption of advanced and sustainable farming prac tices in the UAE.

3.            The International C amel Symposium 2025, hosted by the College of A griculture and Veterinar y Medicine at
   UAE Universit y on Februar y 26, 2025, gathered leading scientist s and industr y exper t s to discuss the latest
   advancement s     in     camel     health,     reproduc tion,     nutrition,     and     welfare.     The     full-day     event     featured     sessions
   on     reproduc tive     technologies,     meat     and     milk     produc tion,     consumer     preferences,     gut     microbiome     studies,
   AI-based     health     monitoring,     and     sustainabilit y.     With     ac tive     par ticipation     from     academia     and     industr y,     the
   symposium reinforced the vital role of camels in food securit y, scientific research, and cultural heritage across
   arid regions, reflec ting the UAE’s leadership in promoting innovation and sustainabilit y in camel science.
4.            The      One      Health      Workshop      on      Avian      Influenza,      held      on      May      7,      2025,      at      the      Ministr y      of      Climate      Change
   and    Environment    (MoCCAE)    Headquar ters    in    Dubai,    was    organized    in    collaboration    with    the    United    Arab
   Emirates     Universit y     (UAEU).     The     workshop     gathered     exper t s     from     the     animal,     human,     and     environmental
   health sectors to streng then the One Health approach in managing Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI).
   The   session   focused   on   enhancing   collaboration   in   disease   sur veillance,   biosecurit y,   public   awareness,   and
   research  to  reduce  the  risks  of  HPAI  to  human  health  and  the  poultr y  industr y.  Discussions  highlighted  the
   global   spread   of   the   H5N1   strain   and   emphasized   the   need   for   coordinated   strategies   to   prevent,   respond

   and food securit y.

Partnerships with external organizations

Under the leadership of Prof. Khaled Masmoudi, the department has established and strengthened collaborations
with  several  prominent  international  organizations,  including  the  International  Center  for Agricultural  Research
in  the  Dry Areas  (ICARDA),  the  Food  and Agriculture  Organization  of  the  United  Nations  (FAO),  and  the Wheat
Initiative.     These      partnerships      focus      on      advancing      research      in      sustainable      agriculture,      crop      improvement,      and
food security, with joint activities that include collaborative projects, capacity-building programs, and knowledge
exchange     initiatives.     Such     strategic     alliances     enhance     the     department’s     global     engagement     and     contribute     to
addressing key agricultural challenges in arid and semi-arid regions.

Impact on the local or global community

The  Animal    Nutrition    Laboratory    contributes    to    the    local    community    by    providing    feed    evaluation    and    testing

local livestock sector, aligning with national goals for food security and agricultural development.

UAE Innovation Month – Workshop on the Future of Animal Science: As part of UAE Innovation Month, Dr. Ebru
Emsen organized and led a workshop titled “Future of Animal Science: Innovations for Sustainable Livestock Pro-
duction”   on   February   3,   2025.  The   event   showcased   cutting-edge   technologies   shaping   the   future   of   livestock
farming, including precision livestock tools, AI-driven health monitoring, smart breeding systems, and sustainable
feeding strategies. Participants explored how innovation enhances productivity, animal welfare, and environmen-
tal sustainability, bridging the gap between science and practical application. The workshop supported the UAE’s
national  vision   for   a   resilient,   technology-driven   agricultural   sector,   fostering   collaboration   among   researchers,
students, and industry professionals.

Colloquium      for      Food      Security      in      the      Drylands      –      Workshop      Presentation:      On      February      14,      2025,      Dr.     Ahmed
Elolimy    delivered    a    presentation    as    part    of    the    Colloquium    for    Food    Security    in    the    Drylands,    focusing    on    the
emerging field of NutriPhysioGenomics and its role in advancing our understanding of gut health in animal mod-
els.  The    session    explored    the    complex    interactions    among    nutrition,    physiology,    and    genomics    in    shaping    live-
stock health and performance. Dr. Elolimy emphasized innovative, integrative scientific approaches aimed at im-
proving animal welfare and productivity in dryland environments. Participants gained valuable insights into how
such   interdisciplinary  methods   can   contribute  to  the   development   of  sustainable   livestock   systems,   supporting
the UAE’s national goals for food security, resilience, and agricultural innovation.

College of Agriculture and Veterinary Medicine Festival 2025: From February 25–27, 2025, the Marine Fisheries
and Animal Science (MFAS) team actively participated in the College of Agriculture and Veterinary Medicine Fes-
tival 2025. Together with Animal Science major students, the team presented interactive and educational displays
highlighting  key  topics  such  as  animal  product  processing,  livestock  breeds,  assisted  reproductive  technologies,
and    organic    animal    farming.   The    booth    attracted    a    large    number    of   visitors    and    successfully    raised    awareness
about sustainable and innovative animal production practices. The team’s participation aligned with the festival’s
mission    to    promote    agricultural    education,    research    excellence,    and    community    engagement   within    the    UAE’s
agricultural sector.

•                                   Over view of major challenges faced during the year
•                                   Lessons learned and strategies for overcoming obstacles

During 2024–2025, the College of Agriculture & Veterinary Medicine (CAVM) navigated several key challenges:
integrating     emerging     technologies     such     as   AI     into     curricula     and     research,     addressing     climate     change     and     sus-
tainability  in  agriculture  and veterinary  practice,  maintaining  a  highly  qualified  and  diverse  faculty,  and  ensuring
students acquire skills aligned with rapidly evolving industry needs.

These challenges offered valuable lessons. The College strengthened its AI program and embedded AI applications
into    core    curricula,    promoted    interdisciplinary    and    international    collaborations,    enhanced    faculty    development
and recruitment, and updated curricula to align with practical, technology-driven competencies. Community en-
gagement and outreach programs
were    strategically    planned    to    max-
imize      impact      on      food      security,      cli-
mate                     resilience,                     and                     sustainable
development.

Through                these                strategies,                CAVM
reinforced                     its                     adaptability,                     inno-
vation,        and        commitment        to        excel-
lence,           preparing           both           faculty           and
students to lead in agriculture, food
science, and veterinary medicine at
national and regional levels.

As we conclude another eventful academic year (2024-2025), I am thrilled
                                                  to   reflect   on   the   remarkable   successes   and  valuable   lessons  we   have   ex-
                                                  perienced together. In this annual report, we take this opportunity to cel-
                                                  ebrate  several  significant  milestones  that  have  shaped  the  College  of  Sci-
                                                  ence throughout the year.

                                                  The most remarkable achievement of the College of Science is its scientific
                                                  research outcomes. Our faculty and students published a total of 722 pa-
                                                  pers in Scopus-indexed journals in 2024, representing an increase of over
                                                  13%   compared   to   2023.   Some   of   these   papers  were   featured   in   prestig-
                                                  ious journals, such as (pls mention a couple of well-known journals). About
                                                  14%    of    these    papers   were    published    in    top    1%    journals,    and    about    70%
                                                  were   published   in   Q1   journals,  which   reflects   the   quality   of   the   research
                                                  carried out in the College. Faculty members also secured numerous inter-
                                                  nal and external research grants totaling around AED 15,304,314.
Prof. Maamar Benkraouda                           Additionally, we established MOUs with several distinguished institutions
Dean, College of Science                          such      as,      Dalian      Institute      &      Lab      on     Advanced      Materials      (China),      Shaanxi

                                                  Normal University & Lab on Advanced Materials (China), Insilico Medicine
(Abu  Dhabi)  Co,  University  of  Insubria  (Italy),  Mediso  Medical  Imaging  Systems  Ltd.  (Hungary).  Our  faculty were
also recognized with nine patents, including five from the U.S. and three from Australia during 2024–2025.

A  particularly  proud  milestone was  the  establishment  of  the  CERN  Data  Center,  achieved  in  collaboration with
the   College   of   Information  Technology   and   the   Division   of   Information  Technology   making   UAE   University   the
first institution in the Gulf region to join the Worldwide Large Hadron Collider (LHC) Computing Grid.

It is in this prestigious collaboration with ATLAS/CERN, that UAEU shared in the “Breakthrough Prize” (which is
known as the Oscars of Science) that was awarded to CERN as a recognition of the cutting-edge research carried
by the researchers of the participating member institutions. ATLAS received $1,000,000 that was decided to be
awarded to excellent prospective PhD students as scholarship.

As part of having an international experience, nine outstanding students from the College participated in a two-

best students was globally selected to participate in the 2-month CERN summer internship.

The College now proudly serves 1,706 undergraduate students, 127 master’s students, and 89 PhD candidates.
This year, we take pride in graduating 119 undergraduate and 56 graduate students.

The faculty and students received several prestigious awards during 2024–2025, including the Khalifa Award for
Education, the Chancellor’s Innovation Award, and the College Excellence Awards, among others.

As we close this successful year, I extend my heartfelt gratitude to every member of our College of Science com-
munity for their dedication, resilience, and pursuit of excellence. Together, we have not only achieved remarkable

Reports From the College Committees (2024-2025)











Research and Graduate Studies Committee                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     Dr. Ruwaya Alkendi

Coordinator: Dr. Ruwaya Alkendi


Members:     Prof.      Rabah      Iratni,      Prof.      Sabir      Bin      Muzaffar,      Prof.    Yaser      Greish,      Dr.      Mabrouk      Hassan,      Prof.      Farrukh
Mukhamedov, Prof. Noureddine Amrane, Dr. Rim Fares.




During  the  academic year  2024–2025,  the  Committee  on  Research  and  Graduate  Studies  implemented  several
initiatives  aimed  at  improving  academic  quality,  enhancing  operational  efficiency,  and  strengthening  the  overall
performance of graduate programs within the College of Science.

One   of   the   key   accomplishments  was   the   optimization   of   courses   and   curricula.  The   committee   recommended
the     consolidation     of     college     requirement     courses     at     both     the     Master’s     and     Ph.D.     levels,     specifically     Research
Methods   I   and   II   and   Ethics   of   Scientific   Research   I   and   II. A   comprehensive   proposal   for   these   changes   is   cur-
rently under preparation.

In the area of policy updates, the committee introduced a new requirement that students seeking postponements
must provide an official letter from their employers to support their requests. This policy aims to promote trans-
parency, accountability, and fairness in handling academic deferments.

The   committee   also   engaged   in   strategic   planning   through   a   detailed   market   study   of   tuition   fee   structures   for
Master’s     programs     across    various     institutions     in     the     UAE.    The     study’s     findings    were     approved     by     the     College
Council and will guide future adjustments to program pricing and competitiveness.

To strengthen student recruitment and outreach, the Office of Research and Graduate Studies launched a dedi-
cated  LinkedIn  account  (COS  UAEU). This  platform  has  enhanced  the  college’s  digital visibility  and  engagement
with prospective students, thereby supporting enrollment and branding efforts.

In terms of program development, the committee initiated the creation of BS–MS track programs in Environmen-
tal Science, Chemistry, and Geosciences. The BS–MS program in Chemistry became active during the academic
year,  while   the   other   two   programs   are   under   review. Additionally,   the   committee   explored   the   introduction   of
non-thesis options for Master’s programs to provide more flexible learning pathways. The Department of Biology

is currently preparing a proposal for the implementation of a non-thesis track.

During     the     academic    year     2024–2025,     the     College     Program     and     Curriculum     Committee     conducted     an     exten-
sive   review   and   revision   of   all   seven   undergraduate   Bachelor   programs   offered   by   the   college,   namely   Biology,
Biochemistry,     Chemistry,     Geosciences,     Mathematics,     Mathematics     of     Data     Science,     and     Physics.    The     revision
primarily focused on restructuring the General Education requirements, which were reduced from thirty-three to
twenty-one credit hours. The reallocated twelve credit hours were distributed among other components of the
respective programs. These revisions were approved and are scheduled for implementation starting in Fall 2025.

In addition to program revisions, the committee reviewed and approved new course proposals submitted by the
Geosciences  Department.  It  also  evaluated  and  endorsed  an  integrated  BS–MS  program  in  Geosciences, which
subsequently      received      approval      from      the      University     Academic      Council      and      is      set      to      commence      in      Fall      2025.
Furthermore, the  committee discussed  a proposal  for a new Bachelor of Science program  in Space Science;  this
proposal is currently undergoing revisions to meet academic and institutional standards. A proposal to revise the
Bachelor of Science in Mathematics of Data Science was also reviewed and approved.

The  committee  considered  several  proposals  related  to  course  modifications,  including  changes  in  prerequisites
and    the    elimination    of    certain    courses.  These    actions    aim    to    streamline    the    curriculum    and    enhance    academic
coherence across programs.
As part of its faculty development initiatives, the committee organized a workshop in November 2024 titled “An
Introduction    to    CurricUNET.”   The   workshop   was    designed    to    familiarize    faculty    members   with    the    university’s
curriculum management system and to improve efficiency in the proposal and review process.

In  summary,  the  Program  and  Curriculum  Committee’s work  during  the  2024–2025  academic year  emphasized
the enhancement of academic quality, modernization of curricula,  and alignment of degree programs with insti-

terdisciplinary learning, and ensure that the college’s programs remain current and competitive within the global
academic landscape.

Internship Program

The internship program is a mandatory requirement of all COS majors. It is an excellent opportunity for COS stu-
dents to get involved in the labor market and acquire some experience from the real work environment. Students
undergo hands-on training at a chosen governmental or private sector institution for a period of 8 weeks. Based
on   their   major,   students   may   opt   to   be   placed   at   municipalities,   forensic   laboratories,   hospitals,   environmental
agencies, oil companies, food control labs, banks, and research centers.

In AY   2024-2025,   259   students   successfully   completed   the   internship   program   (146   students   in   Fall   2024   and
113 students in Spring 2025). The new programs, advising follow up, and internship flexible selections may play
a role in the increase of the internship students.
The COS Internship Office, in coordination with the University Career Readiness Unit, organized a series of work                                  -
shops  under  a  program  called  “Jahez”. This  was  delivered  to  the  internship  students  before  they  started  joining

## PDF page 110 — continuation 2
their  workplaces.  Jahez   program   aims   to   prepare   students  with   the   expectations   of   the  work   environment   and
career requirements. It is offered twice a year, with multiple 4-5 workshops each semester.






110

## PDF page 111
As the entire university activities have returned to normal after the COVID-19 pandemic, the internship program
is now completely face-to-face. However, the workshops of Jahez readiness program were split between online
and onsite attendance due to the timing conflict of some workshops with student’s lab sessions.

Each semester the internship office organizes the Poster Presentation Day where all internship students present
practices     and     skills     they     acquired     and     evaluate     and     discuss     their     internship     experience    with     the     dean,     faculty
members, and students.

ence   took   part   in   a   prestigious   two-week   summer

ness    landscape.   The    program    concluded   with    impactful    project    presentations    and    a    practical    exam,   where    the
students’ efforts were formally recognized. The training was expertly supervised by Ms. Fraya Al Mazrouei.

MSc in Forensic Science. Starting in Fall 2025, the College of Science will launch a new interdisciplinary graduate
program - the Master of Science in Forensic Science. This program encompasses a broad range of interconnected
topics, including the scientific collection, analysis, and presentation of crime-related evidence, as well as the legal
and ethical considerations associated with criminal cases. Its primary aim is to equip students with a solid founda-
tion for professional practice and research in the field. The curriculum combines classroom instruction, extensive
hands-on laboratory training with state-of-the-art techniques and equipment, and independent thesis research.
To graduate, students must complete a minimum of 30 credit hours (CH): 2 CH of core college courses, 13 CH of
forensic science core courses, 6 CH of electives, and 9 CH of thesis work.

## PDF page 118
Research Highlights






UAEU Joins CERN’s Worldwide LHC Computing Grid


United  Arab    Emirates    University    (UAEU)    has    achieved    a    historic    milestone    by    becoming    the    first    institution    in
the    Gulf    region    to    join    CERN’s   Worldwide    LHC    Computing    Grid    (WLCG).  This   was    made    possible    through    the
deployment of a Tier-2 storage site—a 1-petabyte dCache system dedicated to the ATLAS experiment at CERN’s
Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

CERN’s   WLCG   is   a   global   infrastructure   of   1.4   million   CPU   cores   and   1.5   exabytes   of   storage   across   170   sites
in   42   countries,  with   the   CERN   Data   Centre   at   its   core.  This   massive   network   supports   the   analysis   of   particle
collision data from the LHC, the world’s most powerful scientific instrument.



























For  UAEU,  this  breakthrough  opens  new  horizons  in  data-intensive  research  and  high-performance  computing,
benefiting   cross-disciplinary   projects    in   physics,   mathematics,   chemistry,   biology,   and   geosciences.   Within   just
the first month of operation, the UAEU Tier-2 site received nearly 200 TB of LHC data, reflecting its critical role
in global research collaboration.

Dr.       Mohamed       Belfkir,     Assistant       Professor       in       the       Department       of       Physics,       emphasized       the       significance       of       this
achievement:   “This   first-of-its-kind   infrastructure   in   the   Gulf   significantly   enhances   research   capabilities   locally
and globally by providing robust computing and storage resources.”

This initiative underscores UAEU’s commitment to research excellence and international engagement, strength-
ening its position as a leading scientific institution in the region and beyond.







118

## PDF page 119
UAEU Scientists Reveal How Cells Positively Regulate Metabolism
Via Pathway Crosstalk






The Department of Biology (College of Science, UAEU) reported a landmark study led by Dr. Mohammad Tauqeer
Alam in collaboration with Prof. Markus Ralser (Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin) and Dr. Richard Notebaart
(Wageningen University & Research), with Master’s student Sultana Mohammed Al Zubaidi and PhD student Mu-
hammad Ibtisam Nasar as first co-authors. Published in Molecular Systems Biology, the work integrated the yeast
metabolic network with enzyme data from multiple species to construct a comprehensive map of enzyme metab-
olite activator interactions. The study shows that positive, cross-pathway crosstalk is widespread; early steps in
many  pathways  are  preferentially  and  positively  regulated  to  prime  downstream  reactions;  and  highly  activated
enzymes    are    often    embedded    in    secondary    pathways    that    switch    on    under    specific    environmental    conditions.
Collectively, these findings reframe cellular metabolic control around cooperation as well as inhibition and open
new avenues for metabolic engineering, biotechnology, and disease biology.

## PDF page 120
Discovery of Early Supermassive Black Holes





The   College   of   Science   is   proud   to   recognize   the   outstanding   research   achievements   of   Dr.   Muhammad  Abdul
Latif and his team from the Department of Physics, whose groundbreaking work has been published in the pres-
tigious Astrophysical  Journal   Letters   (Top   1–5%,   Impact   Factor   =   11.7).  This   research   has   also   been   featured   in
several leading international space news outlets, marking a significant milestone for the College.

Using  data  from  the James Webb  Space Telescope  (JWST),  the  team  uncovered  evidence  of  a  surprisingly  large
population    of    early    black    holes   with    masses    comparable    to    or    even    exceeding    that    of    the    Milky   Way’s    central
black    hole    approximately    four    million    times    the    mass    of    the    Sun.   These    findings    challenge    existing    theories    of
black  hole  formation  and  suggest  that  such  massive  entities  may  have  originated  through  a  direct  collapse  pro-
cess, in which dense gas clouds collapsed directly into black holes without first forming stars.

The  research  proposes  that  supermassive  black  holes  could  have  formed  as  early  as  200  million years  after  the
Big    Bang,    reshaping    our    understanding    of    early    cosmic    evolution.    Furthermore,    Dr.    Latif    and    his    collaborators
have   derived   the   expected   observational   signatures   of   these   primordial   black   holes,   emphasizing   the   potential
of  upcoming  missions  like  the  Roman  Space Telescope  and  Euclid  to  identify  many  more. The  synergy  between
JWST,   Roman,   and   Euclid  will   provide   a   more   comprehensive  view   of   the   universe’s   earliest   epochs,   advancing
one of the most fundamental questions in astrophysics and cosmology how black holes form and grow.

































120

## PDF page 121
Mosquito Resistance to Insecticides in the UAE





A  groundbreaking  study  conducted  by  resea-rchers  from  UAE  University’s  Department  of  Biology,  in  collabora-
tion with the Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre, has revealed that mosquito populations in the Emirate of Abu Dha-
bi   are   developing   resistance   to   a   key   insecticide,   deltamethrin. The   research  was   published   in   Nature   Scientific
Reports   and   led   by   Professor   Mohammad Al   Deeb,  with   contributions   from   postgraduate   student Amgd   Sayed
Ali. The study focused on the Culex quinquefasciatus species (southern house mosquito), which is not currently
a disease vector in the UAE but is known elsewhere to spread West Nile fever. DNA analysis of 174 adult mos-
quitoes reared from egg clusters collected across Abu Dhabi showed that 18.4% carried two copies of a genetic
mutation     conferring     resistance     to     deltamethrin.     Resistance     was     particularly     prevalent     in     coastal     regions,     with
more than a quarter of the mosquitoes exhibiting mutation.

According to Prof. Al Deeb, the long-term use of insecticides has exerted evolutionary pressure, allowing resist-
ant alleles to spread among mosquito populations. This poses a potential challenge for public health, as resistance
reduces the effectiveness of conventional control measures.

The study emphasizes the importance of long-term monitoring programs and integrated pest management (IPM)
strategies    that    combine    chemical,    biological,    and    environmental    controls,    such    as    the    use    of    natural    mosquito
predators,     habitat     modification,     and     improved     sanitation.     Such     an     approach     is    vital     to     prevent     outbreaks     and
maintain effective vector control.

Furthermore, the research highlights the need for continued vigilance as climate change alters mosquito distribu-
tion and behavior, potentially introducing new vector-borne diseases to the region. Prof. Al Deeb’s team aims to
expand the research to include other mosquito species and explore alternative control strategies, contributing to
the UAE’s preparedness against emerging public health threats.




























                                                                                                                                                  121

## PDF page 122
After the Storm: Assessing Flood Impact





In response to the record-breaking flash floods that struck Al Ain, UAE in April 2024 bringing an unprecedented
250 mm of rainfall within hours, a pioneering study was launched by Professor Hakim Saibi from the Department
of Geoscience, United Arab Emirates University. The research aimed to understand the causes, impacts, and long-
term implications of flooding in arid and semi-arid regions.

Professor  Saibi’s  team  conducted  a  comprehensive  geospatial  assessment  of  the Al Ain  flood,  combining  Senti-
nel-2 satellite data, meteorological data from 16 National Centre of Meteorology (NCM) stations, and topograph-
ic analysis to map the city’s vulnerability. A key innovation of the study was the application of the Index of Turbid
Waters  (ITW),   a  spectral  index  developed   by  Professor  Saibi’s  team   that   distinguishes   between  floodwater  and
permanent water bodies.

The   findings   revealed   a   strong   correlation   between   flood   extent   and   geomorphological  vulnerabilities,   offering
policymakers   critical   insights   into   flood   risk   management   and   urban   resilience. The   ITW   method   demonstrated
high accuracy and reliability, marking a significant advancement in flood mapping for arid environments.
Beyond national significance, the study has global relevance. Collaborative work is underway with researchers in
Italy, Spain, and northeastern Algeria, extending the application of ITW to other regions prone to flash flooding.
The team aims to further enhance the model using higher-resolution hyperspectral satellite data, paving the way
for improved disaster preparedness and sustainable water management strategies worldwide.

Collaboration With Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS)



The    collaboration    project    works    are    going    well    and    here    is    some    of

Project: Detection and determination of carbamate pesticides and re-                                           Prof.  Mohammed Almeetani
lated metabolites in camel milk products of UAE.                                                                  Department of Chemistry

A     method    was     developed,    validated     and     used     to     detect     carbamate     pesticide     residues     in     food     samples     (camel
milk and date fruits) collected from the UAE using UHPLC-MSMS. An optimized liquid-liquid extraction and sol-
id-phase extraction were used to extract carbamate pesticides from the highly complex milk and dates samples.
The detection limit of all studied carbamates was down to 0.01 mg.kg-1. A total of 17 camel milk samples were
studied, and no carbamate residues were found in one sample only. The remaining 16 samples contained at least
one carbamate residue, but the detected concentration for all residues was below the Codexrecommended MRL
(< 10 mg.kg-1) except ethiofencarb residue in three samples was at the borderline.

All date fruit samples contained at least one carbamate residue. While the majority of detected residues were
below their MRLs, carbosulfan was found in 21 samples, propoxur in 2 samples, and carbofuran in 1 sample above
their     MRLs.    The     health     risk     of     carbofuran,     carbaryl,     and     propoxur    was     assessed     for     camel     milk     consumers     by
calculating hazard index (HI) values in pasteurized and raw camel milk and found less than one, therefore camel
milk consumers are not at risk. The UAEU-CAS partnership resulted in the publication of the following articles



1. Rana Morsi, Kilani Ghoudi, Basant Elabyad, Zaina Kadoura, Hind Zeidane, Bayan Al-Meetani, and Mohammed A. Meetani, “HPLC-
MS/MS monitoring and health risk assessment of carbosulfan and its metabolites in date palm fruit (Phoenix dactylifera)”, Sci Rep 14,
28047 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-79871-5.
2. Morsi, R., Ghoudi, K. & Meetani, M.A. Determination and health risk assessment of carbamate pesticide residues in date palm fruits

## PDF page 126 — continuation 2
(Phoenix dactylifera) using QuEChERS method and UHPLC-MS/MS. Sci Rep 14, 13064 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-
63704-6.
3. Rana Morsi, Kilani Ghoudi, Mutamed M. Ayyash, Xiue Jiang, and Mohammed A. Meetani, “Detection of 11 carbamate pesticide
residues in raw and pasteurized camel milk samples using UHPLC-MS/MS: Method development, method validation, and health risk
assessment”. Journal of Diar y Science, 2024, 107(4), 1916-1927. doi: 10.3168/jds.2023-23512.
4. Shaima Askar, Muhammad Usman, Libin Johnson, Delish Thomas, Mohammed A. Meetani "Determination of Multi-Mycotoxins in

## PDF page 127
Toward        high        efficiency        and        large-scale        production        of        flexible
perovskite solar cells


(UAEU-Shaanxi      Normal      University      &      Chinese     Academy      of      Sciences
Collaborative research Project)

                                                                                                                       Dr. Adel Najar
                                                                                                                Department of Physics

The    high    cost    and    long    energy    payback    time    of    silicon    continue    to    constrain    the    global    growth    of    solar    ener-
gy.   Metal-halide   perovskites   offer   a   promising   alternative-abundant,   solution-processable   absorbers   capable   of
delivering  lower  cost  per watt.  However,  the  commercialization  of  perovskite  solar  cells  (PSCs)  still  faces  signif-
icant     challenges,    primarily    due     to    instability    and    performance    fluctuations    caused     by    material    defects     such     as
under-coordinated  Pb²⁺  ions,  halide vacancies,  and  grain-boundary  traps,  as well  as  issues within  the  functional
layers and interfaces of PSCs.

Theoretical   calculations   suggest   that   copper   (Cu)   can   serve   as   an   effective   dopant,   potentially   occupying   inter-
stitial     sites     in     the     perovskite     structure,     thereby     reducing     the     energy     barrier     and     enhancing     carrier     extraction.
Subsequent      experimental      investigations      confirm      that      adding      CuI      as      an      additive      to      MAPbI3-based      perovskite
cells improves optoelectronic properties and overall device performance. Optimizing the amount of Cu (0.01 M)
has   been   found   to   significantly   enhance   crystalline   quality   and   grain   size,   leading   to   improved   light   absorption
and  suppressed  carrier  recombination.  Consequently,  the  power  conversion  efficiency  (PCE)  of  Cu-doped  PSCs
increased from 16.3% to 18.2%. Furthermore, Cu-doped PSCs exhibit higher stabilized power output (SPO) com-
pared  to  pristine  cells. This  study  underscores  the  substantial  benefits  of  Cu  doping  for  advancing  the  develop-
ment of highly efficient PSCs.

In other hand, an effective chelation strategy is reported to suppress harmful physical defects related to untermi-
nated  Cu,  Zn,  and  Sn  sites  by  modifying  the  surface  of  Cu2ZnSn(S,Se)4  (CZTSSe)  films with  sodium  diethyldith-
iocarbamate  (NaDDTC). The  conjoint  theoretical  calculations  and  experimental  results  reveal  that  the  NaDDTC
molecules  can  be  coordinate  to  surface  metal  sites  of  CZTSSe  films via  robust  bidentate  chelating  interactions,
effectively    reducing    surface    undercoordinated    defects    and    passivating    the    electron    trap    states.    Consequently,
the  solar  cell  efficiency  of  the  NaDDTC-treated  device  is  increased  to  as  high  as  13.77%  under  100  mW  cm−2
illumination, with  significant  improvement  in  fill  factor  and  open-circuit voltage. This  surface  chelation  strategy

## PDF page 127 — continuation 2
provides   strong   surface   termination   and   defect   passivation   for   further   development   and   application   of   kester -

## PDF page 128
Memorandum of Understanding between United Arab Emirates
University and Insilico Medicine










On  June   10,   2025,   the   College   of   Science,   United  Arab   Emirates   University   (UAEU)   signed   a   landmark   Memo-
randum   of   Understanding   (MoU)  with   Insilico   Medicine,   establishing   a   strategic   collaboration   in  AI-driven   drug
discovery of small molecule therapies, education, and student development. The partnership was led by Dr. Yasir
Raouf  (Assistant  Professor  of  Chemistry)  as  part  of  initiatives within  the  UAEU  Drug  Discovery  Unit, which  also
includes Dr. Abdelouahid Samadi.

Insilico   Medicine   (www.insilico.com)   is   a   multinational   biotechnology   company   (USD   >$1B)  with   a   regional   HQ
in Abu Dhabi. The company integrates artificial intelligence and experimental pharmacology through its Pharma.
AI  platform  (PandaOmicsTM  for  target  discovery  and  Chemistry42TM  for  molecular  design).  Its  pipeline  of  >30
programs span multiple diseases, including oncology, cardiometabolism, longevity, and immunology.

Its  flagship  ISM001-055  (rentosertib)  program,  for  idiopathic  pulmonary  fibrosis,  met  its  primary  endpoints  in  a
phase IIa trial (NCT05938920), as one of the first examples of an AI-designed molecule to be administered to hu-
mans. The UAEU-Insilico MoU, signed by Dr. Maamar Benkraouda, Dean of the College of Science, and Dr. Alex
Aliper, President/Co-founder of Insilico Medicine, establishes collaboration across 5 key pillars:

•                                   Research: Co-development and academic collaborations on AI-driven medicinal chemistr y.
•                                   Guest Lectures: Par ticipation of Insilico scientist s in UAEU courses and seminars, primarily within the
   increasingly popular CHEM4 42: Introduc tion to Medicinal Chemistr y course.
•                                   Educational                                   Event s:               Organizing hackathons, training                           workshops, and                      innovation challenges to foster
   hands-on learning in computational drug design.
•                                   Internship Program for UAEU Student s: Annual summer placement s at Insilico’s Abu Dhabi headquar ters,
   super vised locally by Dr. Raouf.
•                                   Employment                        Oppor tunities:                            Considering qualified UAEU graduates for roles in bioinformatics, medicinal
   chemistr y, and AI-based research.

The       MoU       signing       ceremony       marked       an       important       mile-
stone        in        building        a        bridge        between        leading        institutions
from    academia    and    industry.   This    strategic    collaboration
also highlights the leadership and forward thinking of
UAEU     in     integrating     academic     science     with     global     lead-
ers       in       biotechnology,       establishing       a       model       that       aims       to
generate  useful  impact  across  research,  education,  talent
development,      and      employability.     This      MoU      also      reflects

## PDF page 128 — continuation 2
the growing nature of the UAE as a regional hub for AI-en-
abled innovation, and will play a critical role in positioning
our college as a leading academic contributor to the bio-
economic strategy of the country as a whole.

## PDF page 129
College     of     Science     Delegation    Visit     to     China:     Strengthening
Research Collaboration and Academic Partnerships










A delegation from the College of Science, headed by the Dean visited five leading universities in China from May
17 to 24, 2025. The delegation comprised Professor Abbas Khaleel, Chairman of the Department of Chemistry;
Professor   Saleh Thaker   Mahmoud,   Chairman   of   the   Department   of   Physics;   Dr. Adama   Diene,   Chairman   of   the
Department of Mathematics; and Professor Adel Najar from the Department of Physics. The visit was organized
to     strengthen      academic      partnerships,      explore     collaborative     research      opportunities,      and     promote     student      and
faculty exchange between the United Arab Emirates University (UAEU) and key Chinese institutions.

The    first    part    of    the   visit    took    place    at    Beihang    University    in    Beijing,   where    the    delegation    participated    in    the
2nd China Emirates Scientific Symposium. During the event, Professor Saleh Thaker delivered a presentation on
“Next-Generation Optoelectronic and Gas Sensors: Innovations in III-V Nitride-Based Devices,” while Professors
Abbas Khaleel and Adel Najar presented their research on catalytic materials and perovskite solar cells. The sym-
posium  provided  an  excellent  platform  for  exchanging  ideas with  Chinese  researchers  and  exploring  shared  sci-
entific interests. The UAEU team also visited the Nanofabrication Laboratory at Beihang University, where they
were     introduced     to     advanced     research     facilities     in     semiconductor     devices     and     nanoscale     materials.     Meetings
with  faculty  members,  including  Professor  Deying  Luo  and  Dr.  Bingjun  Zhu,  led  to  discussions  on  joint  research
proposals and the organization of future workshops focusing on catalysis and materials science.

The     delegation     then     traveled     to     Dalian,    where     they    visited     the     Dalian     Institute     of     Chemical     Physics     (DICP),     a
premier    research    institute    under    the    Chinese   Academy    of    Sciences.   The    UAEU    team   was    hosted    by    Professor
Shengzhong Frank Liu and Dr. Liu Huijuan, Director of Graduate Education. Presentations were exchanged on the
research strengths of both institutions, highlighting areas of mutual interest such as catalysis, renewable energy,
and   chemical   engineering. The  visit   concluded  with   a   tour   of   DICP’s   state-of-the-art   laboratories,  which   show-
cased   the   institute’s   leadership   in   energy   conversion   and   storage   technologies,   including   developments   in   fuel
cells   and  vanadium   redox   flow   batteries.   Both   sides   expressed   interest   in   establishing   joint   graduate   programs,
student exchanges, and collaborative research projects.

On       May       22,       2025,       the       delegation      visited       the       Dalian
University    of   Technology    (DUT),    a    member    of    China’s
Excellence League of top engineering universities. The
team met with senior administrators and the Deans of

## PDF page 129 — continuation 2
the        Schools        of        Chemistry        and        Mathematics.        Discus-
sions focused on fostering partnerships in areas such
as       quantum       information       science,       materials       engineer-
ing,        and        intelligent        chemistry.       The        UAEU        delegation
toured              DUT’s              laboratories,              observing              advanced              re-
search in robotics applied to chemistry, nanomaterials,
and energy-related materials. The visit concluded with
a shared commitment to pursue collaborative research,
faculty mobility, and student exchange initiatives.






                                                                                                                                                              129

## PDF page 130
Later     the     same     day,     the     delegation    visited     Dalian     Minzu     University,    where     they     met    with     the    Vice     Dean     and
faculty   members   of   the   College   of   Physical   and   Material   Engineering.  The   university’s   research   strengths  were
presented   in   the   fields   of   luminescent   materials,   photocatalytic   environmental   remediation,   spintronic   devices,
plasma physics, and solution-processed optoelectronic materials. Discussions centered on the potential for joint
projects in materials synthesis and device engineering, with particular emphasis on energy conversion and envi-
ronmental  sustainability. The visit  provided valuable  insight  into  Dalian  Minzu  University’s  growing  capacity  for
interdisciplinary research and its alignment with the UAEU’s strategic goals.

In addition, Dr. Adama Diene and Professor Maamar Benkraouda visited the Schools of Mathematics at Beihang

separate report detailing these meetings was prepared by Dr. Adama Diene.

ences.     Several     joint     research     proposals    were     initiated

## PDF page 140
The GULF 4 Conference (November 26- 28, 2024)
The GULF 4 conference was held on November 26-28, 2024, under the patronage of the Chancellor of the UAEU
and    Cultural   Advisor    to    the    President    of    the    UAE    (H.E.    Zaki   Anwar    Nusseibeh),   with    the    presence    of    the   Vice
Chancellor (H.E. Prof. Ahmed Al Raeesi) and the honor of having the Minister of State (H.E. Dr. Maitha Bint Salem
Al Shamsi)

The  event was  jointly  organized  by  the  Biology  Department  at  the  College  of  Science,  UAEU  and  the  Canadian
Society  of Aquatic  Ecosystem  health  and  management,  Ontario-Canada. This  conference was  sponsored  by  the
United Arab Emirates University and the Environmental Agency of Abu Dhabi, as well as other private companies
who are serving the scientific research at the Biology Department.

This  edition  of  the  GULF  conference  series  focused  on  the  management  of  the  Gulf’s  ecosystem with  a  special
emphasis on climate change, sustainable regional experiences, and global practices of ecosystems management.

managements. They  come  from  different  Universities,  Research  Institutes  from  East Asia, Africa,  Europe,  North

entific exchange.

                                                       CIT   continued   its   forward   momentum   in   academic   excellence   and   curric-
                                                       ulum innovation. The highlight of the year was the launch of the Bachelor
                                                       of    Science    in    Data    Science    and   Artificial    Intelligence,    an    interdisciplinary
                                                       program   that   immediately   captured   student   interest,   enrolling   more   than
                                                       350      students      in      its      first     year.     This      program      positions      the      college      at      the
forefront of the UAE’s national agenda for AI-driven transformation, equipping graduates with the competencies
to shape the digital future.

Our academic departments also     undertook     comprehensive     updates     to     undergraduate     and     graduate     curricula,
ensuring relevance to current and emerging market demands. Courses such as Advanced Topics in Data Science,
Machine  Learning  for  Embedded  Systems,  and AI  Data  Engineering  reflect  the  college’s  proactive  adaptation  to
global technological trends. The inclusion of a non-thesis option in master’s programs and the launch of GEIT113
– Introduction to AI as a general education course, taken by over 1,500 students, further demonstrate CIT’s ex-
panding academic influence across the university.

CIT continues to uphold the highest standards of quality assurance. All undergraduate programs remain ABET-ac                              -
credited,   while   graduate   programs   are   accredited   by   the   CAA,   ensuring   alignment   with   international   academic

## PDF page 159 — continuation 2
benchmarks.    The     new     BSc     in     Data     Science     and   AI    will     undergo     accreditation     after     graduating     its     first     cohort,
further strengthening CIT’s academic credibility.




The   2024–2025   academic  year   marked   a   new   milestone   in   research   excellence.  The   College   had   20   active   re-
search grants totaling approximately 7 million AED, supporting projects across artificial intelligence, smart cities,
health informatics, and next-generation communication systems.

CIT’s global research impact was remarkable, achieving a Field-Weighted Citation Impact (FWCI) of 6.15, mean-
ing      our      research     was      cited      over      six      times      the     world      average.      Of      195      publications,      16.4%      ranked      among      the
top  10%  most  cited  worldwide,  underscoring  the  outstanding  quality  of  our  scholarly  output.  Faculty  members
demonstrated      leadership      in      emerging      domains      such      as      Brain-Computer      Interfaces,      UAV      Communication      Sys-
tems, Federated Learning, and Blockchain for Healthcare.
